seo.title: Build an MCP Server in Python with FastMCP
seo.description: Learn how to build an MCP server in Python using the FastMCP framework. See how decorator syntax auto-generates JSON schemas for tools.

glossary.definition: A high-level Python framework that abstracts away JSON-RPC boilerplate, allowing developers to build MCP servers using simple function decorators.
A standard format for describing the structure of JSON data. FastMCP automatically generates this from Python type hints and docstrings.
A parameterized URI (like `user://{id}`) that allows a server to dynamically generate and serve resource content based on the client's request.

hook.scenario: You need to expose a complex `calculate_tax` function to an LLM. Historically, this meant spending an hour writing a massive, perfectly nested JSON Schema dictionary by hand, and hoping you didn't miss a bracket.
hook.question: A learner is asked to expose a `calculate_tax` function to an LLM. They start writing a complex nested JSON dictionary by hand. What modern Python feature should they use instead?

mental_model.intuition: FastMCP is like FastAPI, but for AI agents instead of web browsers.
mental_model.description: Building an MCP server from scratch requires manually handling JSON-RPC lifecycles, parsing incoming messages, and hand-writing massive JSON Schema definitions for every tool. FastMCP abstracts all of that away. You write standard Python functions with type hints and a docstring. You add an `@mcp.tool` decorator. FastMCP automatically reads your types and docstrings, generates the required JSON Schema, validates inputs, and handles all the network plumbing.

sections.body: Before FastMCP, exposing a tool to an LLM required writing two things: the actual execution logic, and a massive JSON dictionary describing that logic. If your code changed, you had to manually update the JSON Schema. This was error-prone and tedious.
sections.recap: Manual JSON Schema generation is tedious and error-prone.

sections.body: FastMCP solves this using Python's native type hints and docstrings. When you decorate a function with `@mcp.tool`, the framework inspects your code at runtime. It maps Python types (like `str` or `int`) directly to JSON Schema types, and it extracts your docstring to serve as the tool's description for the LLM.
sections.recap: FastMCP auto-generates JSON Schemas from Python type hints and docstrings.

sections.body: This means your Python docstring is literally the prompt instruction payload the LLM reads. If you write a bad docstring, the LLM won't know how to use your tool. You must write docstrings for the AI, clearly explaining what the tool does and what the parameters mean.
sections.recap: Your Python docstring becomes the LLM's prompt instruction.

sections.body: FastMCP also simplifies Resources. A basic Resource serves static text (like a config file). But what if you need to expose 10,000 user profiles? You shouldn't register 10,000 static resources. Instead, FastMCP supports Resource Templates.
sections.recap: Resources aren't just static files; they can be dynamically generated.

sections.body: Using a parameterized URI template like `user://{id}`, you define a function that dynamically fetches and returns the correct profile whenever the Host requests a specific ID. The Host can list the templates, and the LLM (or user) can request dynamic data on demand.
sections.recap: Resource Templates use parameterized URIs to serve dynamic content.

code_snippets.title: The manual way (Don't do this)
code_snippets.explanation: This boilerplate is fragile. If you change the parameter name in your code, you must remember to update this schema manually, or the LLM will fail to call it.

code_snippets.title: The FastMCP way: Auto-generated schemas
code_snippets.code:
from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP

mcp = FastMCP("TaxServer")

@mcp.tool()
def calculate_tax(amount: float) -> float:
    """Calculates sales tax for a given amount.
    
    Args:
        amount: The purchase amount in USD.
    """
    return amount * 0.08
code_snippets.explanation: This is all you write. FastMCP reads the `float` type hint and the docstring to dynamically generate the exact JSON Schema shown above. The LLM reads your docstring to understand the tool.

code_snippets.title: Dynamic Resource Templates
code_snippets.explanation: Instead of crashing the server by registering 10,000 static resources, this template dynamically handles any request matching the `user://{user_id}` pattern.

common_mistakes.title: Manually writing JSON Schemas
common_mistakes.explanation: Because direct OpenAI function calling historically required passing strict JSON Schema dictionaries, developers assume MCP requires the same boilerplate. Reality: FastMCP completely eliminates this by using Python type hints and standard docstrings to automatically generate the required JSON Schema at runtime.

common_mistakes.title: Assuming Resources are only static
common_mistakes.explanation: Basic tutorials usually demonstrate resources by serving a hardcoded text file. Developers needing to expose thousands of records attempt to write a loop that registers a separate static resource for each one, crashing the server. Reality: FastMCP supports Resource Templates (e.g., `user://{id}`) to dynamically generate content on demand.

recall_questions.q: How does FastMCP map native Python functions to compliant MCP tools?
recall_questions.answer: FastMCP uses an `@mcp.tool` decorator. It inspects the function's type hints and docstring at runtime to automatically generate the compliant JSON-RPC tool schema and handle the network routing.

recall_questions.q: How are JSON Schemas generated dynamically without manual configuration?
recall_questions.answer: FastMCP maps native Python type hints (like `float` or `str`) to JSON Schema types, and parses the function's docstring to populate the description fields that the LLM reads.

recall_questions.q: A developer needs to expose 10,000 unique user profiles and attempts to write a script that registers 10,000 separate static resources, crashing the server. What should they use instead?
recall_questions.answer: They should use a Resource Template. By using a parameterized URI (like `user://{id}`), a single function can dynamically generate and serve the specific profile requested by the client.

recall_questions.q: A learner is asked to expose a `calculate_tax` function to an LLM. They spend 20 minutes writing a complex nested JSON dictionary. What is the modern FastMCP alternative?
recall_questions.answer: Simply writing a standard Python function with type hints and a docstring, and decorating it with `@mcp.tool`. The framework generates the dictionary automatically.

oa_questions.question: How do you avoid writing manual JSON schemas when building an MCP server in Python?
oa_questions.answer: You use a high-level framework like FastMCP. By applying the `@mcp.tool` decorator to a function, FastMCP uses Python's runtime reflection to read the type hints and docstrings, automatically generating the required JSON schema and input validation.
oa_questions.approach: Mention the `@mcp.tool` decorator. Explain that type hints and docstrings are converted directly into the JSON Schema the LLM consumes.

oa_questions.question: How would you serve 10,000 unique user profiles as MCP resources without overloading the server?
oa_questions.answer: Instead of statically registering 10,000 individual resources, I would use a Resource Template. By defining a parameterized URI like `user://{id}`, the FastMCP server can dynamically generate and serve the exact profile requested by the host at runtime.
oa_questions.approach: Contrast static resources with dynamic Resource Templates. Mention parameterized URIs.
